output:
When you buy insurance, you are not handing over every future cost to the insurer. You agree to carry a slice of it yourself. That slice is the deductible.

It works like this. Suppose your car insurance has a £500 deductible and you cause £3,000 of damage. You pay the first £500, and the insurer pays the remaining £2,500. If the repair only came to £400, you would pay all of it and claim nothing.

Think of a shared taxi fare where you always cover the first few miles. Your companion only chips in once the journey runs longer than that.

Why do insurers do this? Partly to discourage tiny claims, which cost more to process than they are worth. Partly to keep you careful, since you have money at stake too.

Your deductible and your premium pull against each other. Choose a high deductible and your monthly premium drops, because the insurer expects to pay out less. Choose a low one and you pay more each month for greater protection.

So pick a figure you could actually afford at short notice. A £2,000 deductible saves little if you cannot find £2,000 on the day.

In short, a deductible is the amount you pay yourself before your insurer starts paying.
